events.title: The election that began the Western Schism
events.shortBlurb: The stormy election of Urban VI led to a rival pope and split Latin Christendom for nearly forty years…
body: On 8 April 1378, in a Rome clamouring for an Italian pope after nearly seventy years of French rule from Avignon, the cardinals in conclave chose Bartolomeo Prignano, Archbishop of Bari, who took the name Urban VI. The election, made under the pressure of a rioting crowd, was accepted at first; but Urban's harsh and imperious temper soon alienated the very men who had chosen him.

Withdrawing to Anagni and then to Fondi, thirteen cardinals declared the election invalid as extorted by fear, and on 20 September 1378 elected Robert of Geneva, who took the name Clement VII and re-established his court at Avignon. France, Scotland, Castile, and Aragon rallied to Clement; England, most of Italy, and the Empire held to Urban.

For thirty-nine years Latin Christendom was divided between two — and after the Council of Pisa in 1409, three — rival obediences, a scandal that set saint against saint, with Catherine of Siena for Urban and Vincent Ferrer for Clement. The Council of Constance ended the division in 1417 with the election of Martin V.

events.title: Trent's decree on Scripture and Tradition
events.shortBlurb: The Council of Trent defined the canon of the Bible and the twin sources of the faith…
body: On 8 April 1546, in its fourth public session, the Council of Trent — opened by Paul III on 13 December 1545 — issued its first dogmatic decree, on the sacred books and the traditions of the Church. Against the reformers' principle of Scripture alone, it taught that the truth and discipline of the Gospel are contained 'in the written books and in the unwritten traditions' received from the apostles.

The same decree fixed the canon of Scripture, the first such definition by a general council, receiving 'entire with all their parts' the books of the Old and New Testaments long read in the Church, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch, and the two books of Maccabees, the so-called deuterocanonical books the reformers had set aside.

It further declared the old Latin Vulgate, hallowed by centuries of use, to be the authentic edition for public reading and disputation, without prejudice to the original texts. These decisions anchored the Catholic answer to the Reformation and governed Catholic teaching on revelation until the Second Vatican Council.
